questions.stem: During emergence, a patient coughs forcefully on the tube and transiently becomes hypertensive. Ventilation is otherwise adequate. Which response carries the greatest risk of creating a new problem after extubation?
options: Using lidocaine as part of a planned strategy to blunt coughing
Giving a large opioid bolus solely to normalize the transient vital-sign response
Coordinating extubation timing with the surgical team
questions.explanation: Transient coughing-related hypertension at emergence is not by itself an indication for a large opioid bolus. Near extubation, excess opioid can outlast airway stimulation and produce delayed hypoventilation or obstruction after the endotracheal tube is removed.

questions.stem: A patient with a painful spine fusion is transported to PACU before the receiving nurse can immediately access ordered rescue analgesics. Which preparation best prevents an avoidable gap in pain treatment during handoff?
options: Start a PCA solely for the transport interval
Bring nothing because PACU pharmacy will eventually supply them
Bring appropriate medications needed to treat pain during transport/handoff
Leave all analgesics in the OR
questions.explanation: Analgesic responsibility continues through transport and handoff. If rescue medication will not be immediately available in PACU, carrying an appropriate secured medication supply prevents an avoidable treatment gap while maintaining controlled-substance accountability.

questions.stem: At PACU handoff, opioid doses are documented but no assessment of the patient's current pain or functional limitation appears in the record. Which missing element is necessary to judge treatment effectiveness?
questions.explanation: Medication administration alone does not show whether treatment worked. Handoff should include the current validated pain assessment, relevant functional limitation, sedation/respiratory status, drugs and regional techniques used, and response so the receiving team can safely continue the plan.

questions.stem: The record shows fentanyl 100 mcg given, but 250 mcg was signed out and no waste was recorded. Why does this matter?
options: Waste can be documented at the end of the day
questions.explanation: Controlled-substance records must reconcile the amount obtained with the amount administered, wasted, or returned. A discrepancy between signed-out fentanyl and documented administration/waste is both a medication-safety and diversion-accountability problem that requires resolution.

questions.stem: A total-knee patient reaches PACU with severe uncontrolled pain despite stable physiology. Which downstream effect is MOST likely?
options: Faster discharge because severe pain increases alertness
Prolonged PACU recovery because analgesia must be established before discharge criteria are met
questions.explanation: Severe uncontrolled pain can prevent mobilization, breathing exercises, oral intake, or satisfaction of discharge criteria and often requires repeated rescue dosing and reassessment. Arriving in PACU without an effective analgesic plan can therefore prolong recovery even when vital signs are stable.

questions.stem: Which FOUR programming elements are fundamental to a demand-only IV PCA prescription? (Select 4)
options: Dose limit when used by the institution/device
Patient weight as the only dosing variable
questions.explanation: A demand-only PCA order must clearly identify the opioid/concentration, patient demand dose, lockout interval, and any dose limit used by the institution. A continuous basal infusion is a separate optional setting and generally adds respiratory risk in opioid-naive patients.

questions.stem: Which statement about PCA programming is most accurate?
options: Patient weight and diagnosis are sufficient programming instructions
Every PCA requires a continuous background infusion
The order must clearly define the drug/concentration, demand dose, lockout, applicable limits, and whether a background infusion is intentionally used or omitted
A lockout interval is optional if the demand dose is small
questions.explanation: PCA safety depends on unambiguous programming of drug/concentration, demand dose, lockout, dose limits, and whether a basal infusion is intentionally present. The background infusion should never be assumed to be a required component of PCA therapy.

questions.stem: An opioid-naive patient requires PCA after hysterectomy and can activate the device appropriately. Which order feature should generally be avoided because it adds opioid exposure independent of patient demand?
questions.explanation: PCA allows the patient to self-administer small IV opioid doses within programmed safety limits, reducing delays between pain onset and treatment. Only the patient should activate the demand button unless a specifically authorized protocol provides otherwise, because proxy dosing can bypass the patient's sedation-limited self-protection.

questions.stem: In PCA programming, what is the minimum time that must elapse before another patient-triggered dose can be delivered called?
questions.explanation: A basal opioid infusion continues even when an opioid-naive patient becomes sleepy and stops pressing the PCA button, removing an important feedback safeguard. This can increase cumulative opioid exposure and respiratory depression, especially during sleep or in OSA.

questions.stem: In PCA programming, what term describes opioid delivered continuously regardless of patient button presses?
questions.explanation: PCA-related respiratory risk rises with basal infusions, concurrent sedatives, OSA, advanced age, organ dysfunction, and other factors that increase opioid sensitivity or accumulation. Monitoring intensity should match the patient's risk and institutional protocol rather than relying on the PCA lockout alone.

questions.stem: In PCA therapy, what is the initial clinician-administered dose used to establish analgesia before patient demand dosing called?
questions.explanation: Continuous pulse oximetry can detect oxygenation failure but supplemental oxygen may delay desaturation during opioid hypoventilation. Ventilation assessment, including capnography when indicated and feasible, adds earlier information about apnea or hypoventilation in high-risk patients.

questions.stem: In PCA therapy, what is the patient-triggered amount delivered after an eligible button press called?
questions.explanation: Sedation often precedes severe opioid-induced respiratory depression. A patient who is increasingly difficult to arouse after PCA dosing should be assessed immediately for airway patency and ventilation, with opioid delivery stopped/reduced and reversal/support provided as clinically indicated.

questions.stem: A hydromorphone PCA order specifies a demand dose but omits the lockout interval. Why is this omission dangerous?
options: Repeated successful demands could deliver excessive opioid and cause respiratory depression
The pump will necessarily underdose the patient
The PCA cannot contain hydromorphone without a basal infusion
The omission only affects documentation, not dosing
questions.explanation: Neuraxial opioids can produce respiratory depression, pruritus, nausea, and urinary retention without the dense motor block expected from local anesthetic. Hydrophilic morphine has delayed rostral spread and therefore requires prolonged respiratory surveillance.

questions.stem: You plan dexamethasone for PONV and analgesia during a 2-hour laparoscopic case. What should guide when you give it?
options: Giving it with the NSAID at the end of the case
Its slow onset and your PONV and analgesic goals
Giving it at emergence with the antiemetics
questions.explanation: Lipophilic neuraxial opioids such as fentanyl and sufentanil have rapid spinal uptake and relatively rapid onset, while hydrophilic morphine remains in CSF longer and can provide prolonged analgesia with delayed respiratory-depression risk. Drug choice should match desired duration and monitoring capability.

questions.stem: A ketamine infusion is supplying an important component of analgesia during a long case. Which maintenance check prevents an unplanned interruption near the end of surgery?
options: Confirm only that the line has a label
Obtain surgeon approval for every infusion-rate check
Verify enough drug remains for the intended duration
questions.explanation: Epidural local anesthetic can produce sympathectomy, sensory block, and motor block depending on concentration and level. Hypotension or unexpected motor weakness should prompt assessment of block extent, dose, catheter position, and other causes rather than simply increasing the infusion.

questions.stem: Near emergence, why can spontaneous respiratory rate be useful when titrating the final opioid doses?
options: A rising carbon dioxide level is intentionally used to deepen anesthesia
The goal is to create apnea before extubation
It eliminates the need to assess other opioid effects
It helps balance residual analgesic effect against ventilatory depression
questions.explanation: Unexpected dense motor block from a postoperative epidural can signal excessive local-anesthetic effect or catheter migration and may impair mobility or mask neurologic findings. The infusion and catheter should be reassessed promptly rather than treating motor weakness as an expected analgesic endpoint.

questions.stem: A PACU regimen contains only small hydromorphone rescue doses for a patient expected to have substantial ongoing pain. Which planning principle best avoids repeated breakthrough-pain cycles?
options: Provide an appropriate strategy for both immediate rescue and sustained analgesic coverage
Use only short-acting rescue opioid indefinitely
Use only long-acting opioid without rescue capability
Avoid opioids regardless of pain severity
questions.explanation: Anticoagulant timing around neuraxial catheter placement and removal affects spinal/epidural hematoma risk. The plan must follow current drug-specific neuraxial guidelines and account for renal function, traumatic placement, concurrent hemostatic drugs, and the exact timing of doses.

questions.stem: A patient arrives in PACU with epidural and continuous peripheral nerve-block catheters, but pharmacy needs an hour to prepare both infusions. Which systems failure created the analgesic gap?
options: Failure to start every catheter infusion in the OR
Failure to coordinate needed infusions with pharmacy in advance
Failure to delay analgesia until postoperative day 1
Failure to substitute IV opioids for regional analgesia
questions.explanation: New severe back pain, progressive motor or sensory deficit, or bowel/bladder dysfunction after neuraxial instrumentation can indicate compressive spinal hematoma. This is a time-sensitive neurologic emergency requiring immediate evaluation and urgent imaging/decompression pathways rather than routine analgesic adjustment.

questions.stem: You plan a ketamine and lidocaine infusion for a spine case. When should the drips start?
questions.explanation: Continuous peripheral nerve blocks can provide strong site-specific analgesia with less systemic opioid exposure, but catheter migration, infection, local-anesthetic toxicity, motor weakness, and block-specific nerve effects remain possible. Discharge education must include protection of the insensate limb and when to seek help.

questions.stem: Which infusions does the maintenance slide list? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Motor weakness from a peripheral block can increase fall risk even when analgesia is excellent. Technique and concentration should be selected to balance analgesia with preservation of function, and ambulation precautions should match the expected motor effect.

questions.stem: A fentanyl infusion has run for 8 hours and is still infusing as closure begins. Which concern should MOST influence when it is stopped?
options: Late discontinuation reliably prevents emergence hypertension without respiratory cost
Longer infusion duration makes fentanyl clear faster
Stopping fentanyl causes immediate physiologic withdrawal in opioid-naive patients
Accumulation can lengthen context-sensitive recovery and delay emergence
questions.explanation: A numb extremity is vulnerable to pressure, heat, and mechanical injury because protective sensation is reduced. Patients discharged with an active block should receive explicit instructions about limb protection, weight bearing, fall prevention, catheter care, and signs of toxicity or neurologic concern.

questions.stem: A patient receiving intrathecal morphine and a bupivacaine block develops several problems. Which are known adverse effects of these analgesics? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity can begin with circumoral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, agitation, or seizures and progress to conduction disturbance, arrhythmia, hypotension, or cardiovascular collapse. Suspected LAST requires immediate airway/circulatory support and lipid-emulsion therapy according to current protocols.

questions.stem: Hours after neuraxial morphine, a patient develops pruritus followed by respiratory slowing. Which pharmacologic behavior BEST explains the delayed respiratory risk?
options: Cephalad cerebrospinal-fluid spread with central opioid-receptor effect
Slow absorption from a peripheral injection site
Local anesthetic migration to the brainstem
questions.explanation: Intravascular injection can produce abrupt high local-anesthetic concentrations before total dose limits are reached. Incremental injection, aspiration, appropriate test dosing when relevant, monitoring, and communication reduce risk but cannot eliminate it.

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes after intrathecal fentanyl, a patient becomes markedly bradypneic. Which neuraxial-opioid pattern best explains the timing?
options: Delayed respiratory depression from a hydrophilic opioid
Early respiratory depression from a lipophilic opioid
questions.explanation: Maximum local-anesthetic dose tables are safety guides rather than guarantees of toxicity-free dosing. Patient size, age, pregnancy, organ dysfunction, injection site vascularity, epinephrine use, and cumulative exposure from all sources can change systemic concentration and risk.

questions.stem: A patient receives intrathecal morphine at 0800 and develops RR 6/min at 2000. Which property best explains this delayed respiratory-depression pattern?
options: Delayed cephalad effect of hydrophilic morphine
questions.explanation: Epinephrine can reduce systemic absorption of some local anesthetics and increase the conventional maximum recommended dose, but it does not make unlimited dosing safe. Total exposure, injection site, comorbidities, and signs of intravascular injection still determine risk.

questions.stem: Refer to the neuraxial timing figure. Which curve fits intrathecal morphine?
options: Opioid X, with an early peak risk
Opioid Y, with a delayed peak risk
questions.explanation: Dose calculations must use the actual drug concentration: 1% solution equals 10 mg/mL, 0.5% equals 5 mg/mL, and so forth. Converting percentage to mg/mL before multiplying by volume prevents common local-anesthetic dosing errors.

questions.stem: Refer to the neuraxial timing figure. Which curve fits intrathecal fentanyl?
options: Opioid X, with an early peak risk
Opioid Y, with a delayed peak risk
questions.explanation: Cumulative local-anesthetic exposure includes every route and administrator. A regional block plus surgeon infiltration can exceed a recommended limit even when each individual dose appears acceptable, so the total milligram dose should be reconciled before additional drug is given.

questions.stem: A patient has troublesome pruritus after intrathecal morphine but remains awake with normal ventilation and excellent analgesia. Which strategy can treat neuraxial opioid pruritus while limiting loss of analgesia?
options: Large naloxone boluses until all opioid effects disappear
Carefully titrated low-dose naloxone or another evidence-based antipruritic strategy
Flumazenil as the primary opioid antagonist
questions.explanation: Lipid emulsion is a core component of resuscitation for severe LAST, but treatment also requires airway/ventilatory support, seizure control, modified cardiovascular resuscitation, and avoidance of drugs that can worsen toxicity. Teams performing regional anesthesia should have an immediately accessible LAST protocol and lipid supply.

questions.stem: A PACU patient is hypoventilating after both midazolam and hydromorphone. What is the immediate management priority?
options: Give naloxone only after oxygen saturation falls
Give flumazenil automatically before assessing ventilation
Support the airway and ventilation, stop contributing sedatives, then use drug-specific antagonists selectively based on likely cause and patient risk
Use flumazenil to reverse both drugs
questions.explanation: LAST-related cardiac arrest is managed with high-quality resuscitation plus lipid emulsion and modifications to standard ACLS because local-anesthetic toxicity alters myocardial conduction and contractility. Current LAST guidance should be followed rather than assuming routine arrest pharmacology is sufficient.

questions.stem: A patient is oversedated after midazolam. You give flumazenil 0.2 mg IV every minute. After the fourth dose, the patient is still drowsy. How much more can you give before reaching the typical 1 mg total?
options: None; the maximum has been reached
questions.explanation: Bupivacaine is particularly cardiotoxic because of strong, persistent binding to cardiac sodium channels. Severe toxicity can produce refractory ventricular arrhythmias and cardiovascular collapse, making prevention and rapid lipid-based resuscitation especially important.

questions.stem: A patient is deeply sedated and bradycardic after excessive dexmedetomidine. Why must management rely mainly on supportive care and treatment of hemodynamic effects?
options: There is no routinely available human reversal agent for dexmedetomidine
Dexmedetomidine is a strong mu-opioid agonist
questions.explanation: Ropivacaine is generally less cardiotoxic than bupivacaine but can still cause seizures, arrhythmias, or cardiovascular collapse at sufficiently high systemic concentrations. Relative safety does not eliminate the need for dose limits and LAST preparedness.

questions.stem: Dexmedetomidine, ketamine, and hydromorphone are combined at full usual doses. The patient becomes more sedated and hypotensive than expected from any one agent. Which principle BEST explains this?
options: Different drug classes cannot produce additive effects
Pharmacodynamic synergy can amplify both desired effects and adverse effects
Combining agents reliably shortens each drug's duration
questions.explanation: Ultrasound can improve needle visualization and may reduce vascular puncture or required local-anesthetic volume in some blocks, but it does not eliminate intravascular injection or systemic absorption. Standard incremental-injection and toxicity precautions remain necessary.

questions.stem: A multimodal spine plan includes dexmedetomidine, hydromorphone, and ketamine. How should the presence of overlapping analgesic and sedative effects influence dosing?
options: Reduce only ketamine because opioids do not interact with alpha-2 agonists
Use the full standalone dose of every agent
Use lower individualized doses of the component agents
No dose adjustment is needed when mechanisms differ
questions.explanation: A negative aspiration test cannot exclude intravascular needle or catheter position because the vessel may collapse or the needle tip may migrate. Incremental dosing with ongoing clinical monitoring remains necessary even after negative aspiration.

questions.stem: A patient becomes hypotensive after analgesic administration. What is the best immediate approach?
options: Give naloxone for all postoperative hypotension
Give a vasopressor without any assessment in every case
Assume the opioid is the sole cause
Assess perfusion and likely cause, including heart rate/rhythm, volume status, anesthetic effects, and other contributors, while treating clinically significant hypotension
questions.explanation: Early CNS symptoms can precede cardiovascular collapse in LAST, but heavily sedated or anesthetized patients may not report warning symptoms. Continuous physiologic monitoring and attention to unexplained hemodynamic or electrical changes are therefore essential during regional techniques.

questions.stem: A patient becomes bradycardic after analgesics. What is the FIRST assessment?
questions.explanation: Seizure from LAST increases oxygen consumption and acidosis, which can worsen local-anesthetic cardiotoxicity. Immediate oxygenation/ventilation and benzodiazepine treatment are priorities while lipid-emulsion therapy and circulatory support are initiated as indicated.

questions.stem: A patient develops symptomatic bradycardia with hypotension after sedative-analgesic administration. Which management principle is most appropriate?
options: Glycopyrrolate is mandatory for every episode
Reduce contributing drugs, assess the cause, support perfusion, and use an appropriate chronotropic/vasopressor treatment based on the clinical situation
Ephedrine is the only acceptable treatment
Observe without intervention whenever the heart rate is above 30/min
questions.explanation: Local-anesthetic dose should generally be calculated using an appropriate weight scalar and capped at accepted maximums while accounting for patient-specific risk and cumulative dosing. Obesity does not justify proportionally unlimited milligram dosing simply because total body weight is high.

questions.stem: A patient has excellent analgesia after morphine but develops repeated nausea and vomiting without respiratory depression or other toxicity. Which treatment best preserves the useful opioid effect?
questions.explanation: Epinephrine-containing local-anesthetic solutions may be undesirable where intense vasoconstriction could threaten perfusion or in patients particularly vulnerable to adrenergic effects. The decision should reflect site, concentration, dose, vascular status, and patient comorbidities rather than a blanket rule.

questions.stem: After morphine, a patient develops isolated generalized itching without urticaria, facial swelling, bronchospasm, or hypotension. Which interpretation is MOST appropriate?
options: Anaphylaxis requiring permanent avoidance of every opioid
A common opioid adverse effect rather than evidence of true allergy
questions.explanation: Conventional maximum recommended doses are commonly expressed in mg/kg but should be treated as approximate safety ceilings rather than thresholds below which toxicity is impossible. Patient factors, injection site, cumulative dosing, and inadvertent intravascular injection can produce toxicity at lower totals.

questions.stem: A 70 kg patient will receive lidocaine for infiltration. What are the maximum doses plain and with epinephrine?
options: About 315 mg plain and 490 mg with epinephrine
About 490 mg plain and 315 mg with epinephrine
About 175 mg plain and 210 mg with epinephrine
About 700 mg plain and 1,050 mg with epinephrine
questions.explanation: Using the conventional limits in the question, 4.5 mg/kg × 70 kg gives 315 mg plain lidocaine and 7 mg/kg × 70 kg gives 490 mg with epinephrine. These calculated maxima do not replace clinical judgment or cumulative-dose tracking.

questions.stem: What must be available wherever regional anesthesia is given? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Regional anesthesia should be performed where oxygenation and ventilation can be supported, vascular access and resuscitation drugs are available, and LAST can be treated immediately. The exact equipment set should match the block and environment, but airway-rescue capability and lipid emulsion are core preparedness elements.

questions.stem: A clinician proposes performing an interscalene block in an unmonitored area without immediate airway equipment or lipid emulsion. Which principle should determine the response?
options: An awake patient makes monitoring and rescue capability unnecessary
Regional anesthesia should be performed where complications can be recognized and resuscitation can begin immediately
Lipid emulsion is unnecessary for peripheral blocks
Convenience outweighs rescue readiness for single-shot blocks
questions.explanation: An interscalene block can cause local-anesthetic toxicity, high neuraxial spread, phrenic impairment, pneumothorax, or other complications that may require immediate resuscitation. Performing it in an unmonitored area without airway equipment or lipid emulsion removes the ability to recognize and treat those complications promptly.

questions.stem: A 60 kg patient receives 150 mg lidocaine for a field block, and the surgeon wants 20 mL of 1% lidocaine more. Using the 4.5 mg/kg plain limit, what should you do?
options: Proceed; each injection has its own limit
Proceed if the additional dose is given slowly
questions.explanation: Twenty milliliters of 1% lidocaine contains 200 mg. Adding that to the existing 150 mg gives 350 mg, which exceeds the question's conventional plain-lidocaine limit of 4.5 mg/kg × 60 kg = 270 mg; doses from all sources must be counted cumulatively.

questions.stem: An excessively sedated patient received both a benzodiazepine and opioid. Ventilation is being supported and preserving analgesia is desirable. Which reversal sequence is emphasized in the source?
options: Use ketamine as a respiratory reversal agent
Give a large naloxone dose first regardless of analgesic need
Increase opioid to prevent withdrawal before reversal
Consider flumazenil for the benzodiazepine before titrating naloxone
questions.explanation: When both benzodiazepine and opioid contribute to oversedation, ventilation remains the immediate priority. If preserving opioid analgesia is important and benzodiazepine effect is substantial, cautious flumazenil may reduce sedation before naloxone is titrated, but seizure/withdrawal risk and the actual drug contribution must be considered.

questions.stem: A patient with an epidural containing hydromorphone has intense itching but good pain relief. What is likely to help?
questions.explanation: Neuraxial opioid pruritus is primarily centrally mediated through opioid receptors rather than histamine release. Very low-dose naloxone can reduce mu-mediated itching while attempting to preserve analgesia, although other antipruritic strategies may also be used.

questions.stem: A patient taking opioids daily develops yawning, sweating, diarrhea, and autonomic symptoms after an abrupt missed dose; symptoms resolve when the opioid is restored. Which phenomenon is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Physical dependence is a physiologic adaptation in which abrupt cessation or antagonism produces a withdrawal syndrome. Relief of yawning, sweating, diarrhea, and autonomic symptoms when the opioid is restored supports dependence rather than tolerance or opioid use disorder by itself.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A chronic opioid user now requires 20 mg oxycodone to achieve the analgesia previously produced by 10 mg, without withdrawal symptoms or compulsive use behavior. Which phenomenon is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Tolerance means a larger dose is required to produce an effect previously achieved with a smaller dose. It is distinct from physical dependence, which is demonstrated by withdrawal, and from opioid use disorder, which is defined by maladaptive behavioral criteria rather than dose requirement alone.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A patient requires progressively larger opioid concentrations to achieve the same analgesic response, shifting the dose-response curve to the right. Which adaptation does this represent?
questions.explanation: A rightward shift in the dose-response relationship means higher drug concentrations are needed to achieve the same effect, which is pharmacodynamic tolerance. This can occur through receptor and downstream signaling adaptations during chronic opioid exposure.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A patient requires progressively larger opioid doses for the same analgesia but has never developed withdrawal when doses are missed. Which conclusion is MOST accurate?
options: Tolerance can exist without physical dependence
Tolerance and dependence are physiologically identical
questions.explanation: Tolerance and physical dependence are related adaptations but neither requires the other to be demonstrated in a particular patient. Increasing dose requirement establishes tolerance; dependence specifically requires a withdrawal syndrome after reduction, cessation, or antagonism.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: What are features of opioid withdrawal? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Opioid withdrawal commonly produces autonomic hyperactivity and gastrointestinal symptoms such as tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, cramping, nausea/vomiting, and diarrhea. It is usually intensely uncomfortable but differs physiologically from opioid intoxication, which causes sedation and respiratory depression.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A chronic opioid user requires progressively larger doses despite unchanged painful pathology. Which receptor adaptation most directly contributes to pharmacodynamic tolerance?
questions.explanation: Chronic opioid exposure can cause receptor phosphorylation, internalization/downregulation, and altered G-protein signaling, reducing response to the same agonist concentration. These pharmacodynamic changes contribute to the rightward dose-response shift of tolerance.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A patient taking oxycodone 60 mg/day presents for lumbar fusion. Which four actions BEST prevent both withdrawal and undertreatment? (Select 4)
options: Identify the degree of opioid dependence
Plan when chronic medications will resume
Stop all home opioids before surgery
Avoid ketamine because of opioid tolerance
questions.explanation: Perioperative planning for chronic opioid therapy should identify the patient's actual baseline exposure and dependence, prevent withdrawal by continuing or replacing that baseline, add multimodal/regional analgesia when feasible, and separately titrate additional medication for new surgical pain.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: For the same opioid-tolerant patient, which adjuncts are appropriate? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Ketamine, magnesium, gabapentinoids, and selected muscle-relaxant or other adjuvant therapies can reduce reliance on escalating opioids in tolerant patients when matched to the pain mechanism. Each has distinct sedation, hemodynamic, renal, or drug-interaction risks, so adjuncts should be selected rather than automatically stacked.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient taking duloxetine will receive ondansetron for PONV prophylaxis and requests tramadol postoperatively. Which interaction should MOST influence the plan?
options: Ondansetron converts tramadol into a more potent opioid metabolite
Tramadol primarily increases surgical bleeding when combined with duloxetine
Tramadol adds serotonergic activity and may interact with duloxetine; ondansetron may also reduce its analgesic effect
questions.explanation: Tramadol inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake in addition to opioid activity, so combining it with duloxetine increases serotonergic toxicity risk. Its analgesia also depends partly on CYP2D6 activation, and multiple perioperative drug interactions make it less predictable than a simple direct-acting opioid.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A physically opioid-dependent patient takes scheduled oxycodone and is NPO for surgery. Which principle should guide the morning-of-surgery plan?
options: Replace the opioid with a mixed agonist-antagonist
Withhold all opioid because fasting eliminates baseline requirements
Reduce the usual dose by half in every patient
Maintain the patient's usual baseline opioid exposure or provide an appropriate equivalent to prevent withdrawal
questions.explanation: Abruptly withholding baseline opioid from a physically dependent patient can precipitate withdrawal and complicate perioperative pain control. The usual opioid exposure should generally be continued or replaced with an appropriate equivalent while additional surgical analgesia is managed separately.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: An opioid-tolerant patient presents for major surgery. How should postoperative opioid requirements be anticipated?
options: Expect potentially higher requirements than in an opioid-naive patient, but calculate baseline exposure and titrate rescue dosing to individual response rather than applying a fixed percentage increase
Increase every opioid dose by exactly 30%
Use the same doses as an opioid-naive patient because tolerance affects only euphoria
questions.explanation: Opioid-tolerant patients often require more opioid for acute surgical pain than opioid-naive patients, but the increase is highly variable. Baseline exposure should be maintained/replaced, multimodal and regional techniques used when appropriate, and supplemental opioid titrated to pain, function, sedation, and ventilation rather than a fixed percentage rule.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A patient maintained on buprenorphine has substantial postoperative pain despite multimodal therapy. Which supplemental opioid strategy BEST matches the source?
options: Use nalbuphine because mu antagonism improves buprenorphine analgesia
Use a full agonist such as hydromorphone, fentanyl, or morphine as needed
Give naltrexone before a full agonist
Avoid all full agonists because they cannot provide any analgesia
questions.explanation: Buprenorphine's high-affinity partial mu agonism can make supplemental analgesia challenging, but full mu agonists with high receptor affinity such as hydromorphone or fentanyl can still be titrated when needed as part of a multimodal plan. Perioperative buprenorphine management should follow the patient's maintenance indication and current institutional guidance rather than automatic discontinuation.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: Which drugs should be AVOIDED in opioid-dependent patients? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Mixed agonist-antagonist opioids such as nalbuphine, butorphanol, and pentazocine can antagonize mu-receptor effects while activating other opioid receptors. In a patient physically dependent on a full mu agonist, that displacement can precipitate acute withdrawal.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A patient physically dependent on oxycodone receives butorphanol and rapidly develops diaphoresis, agitation, abdominal cramping, and tachycardia. What is the BEST explanation?
options: The patient developed local anesthetic systemic toxicity
Additive full-mu agonism produced opioid overdose
Mu antagonism from a mixed agonist-antagonist precipitated withdrawal
questions.explanation: Butorphanol has mixed agonist-antagonist activity and can reduce mu-receptor signaling in a patient dependent on full mu agonism. The abrupt decrease in effective mu stimulation can precipitate autonomic and gastrointestinal withdrawal symptoms despite administration of an opioid-class drug.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: Buprenorphine provides mu-receptor analgesia but exhibits a ceiling on some opioid effects. Which receptor behavior best explains this?
questions.explanation: A partial agonist binds the receptor but produces less maximal signaling than a full agonist even with high receptor occupancy. Buprenorphine's high-affinity partial mu agonism therefore creates a ceiling on some opioid effects while still providing analgesia and suppressing withdrawal.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: Butorphanol provides kappa agonism while antagonizing mu receptors, a combination that can precipitate withdrawal in mu-dependent patients. How is it classified?
questions.explanation: Butorphanol acts primarily as a kappa agonist with mu-antagonist/partial-antagonist properties, so it is classified as a mixed agonist-antagonist. Its mu-antagonist behavior explains why it can precipitate withdrawal in patients dependent on full mu agonists.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A patient takes buprenorphine, and another takes butorphanol. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
options: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist; butorphanol is a mixed agonist-antagonist
Buprenorphine is a mixed agonist-antagonist; butorphanol is a partial agonist
questions.explanation: A partial agonist activates a receptor submaximally; a mixed agonist-antagonist is an agonist at one receptor and antagonist at another.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A highly opioid-tolerant patient receives escalating hydromorphone with diminishing benefit and increasing adverse effects. Which strategy may improve analgesic responsiveness without simply escalating the same opioid?
options: Add a basal infusion of the same opioid regardless of current exposure
questions.explanation: When escalating one opioid produces diminishing analgesic benefit with increasing toxicity, switching to a different opioid can exploit incomplete cross-tolerance and different receptor/pharmacokinetic properties. Methadone may be useful in selected highly tolerant patients because of mu agonism and NMDA antagonism, but conversion is complex and requires conservative dosing and expertise.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: An opioid-tolerant patient is being considered for perioperative gabapentin. Which principle is most appropriate?
options: Renal function does not affect gabapentin dosing
Give more than 800–1,000 mg to every opioid-tolerant patient
Gabapentin has no clinically important respiratory interaction with opioids
Use patient-specific dosing and weigh opioid-sparing benefit against sedation, respiratory risk, age, renal function, and concomitant CNS depressants
questions.explanation: Gabapentinoids can reduce pain or opioid use in selected patients but can also increase sedation and respiratory depression, especially with opioids and in higher-risk patients. Gabapentin is renally eliminated, so dosing should be individualized rather than using a mandatory high preoperative dose.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: Two patients need PCA after major surgery. One is opioid-naive; the other has substantial chronic opioid tolerance. In which patient may a basal infusion reasonably be considered?
options: The opioid-tolerant patient after accounting for baseline requirements
The opioid-naive patient because a basal rate is safer
Both patients because basal infusions reduce respiratory depression
questions.explanation: A basal PCA infusion may be appropriate in selected opioid-tolerant patients when it replaces part of a known baseline opioid requirement. In opioid-naive patients, a background infusion can continue dosing during sleep or sedation and increases respiratory-depression risk without the demand-button feedback safeguard.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A highly opioid-tolerant patient needs a major spine fusion. Which overall strategy is most appropriate?
options: Abruptly stop baseline opioids and rely on acetaminophen alone
Continue/replace baseline opioid exposure, use multimodal and regional techniques when feasible, and individualize supplemental opioid therapy
Use a mixed agonist-antagonist to reverse tolerance
Escalate one full agonist without adding other analgesic mechanisms
questions.explanation: The opioid-tolerant patient has two separate needs: continuation or replacement of baseline opioid to prevent withdrawal and additional treatment for new surgical pain. Multimodal and regional techniques can reduce supplemental opioid burden, while rescue dosing should be individualized to response and adverse effects.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient arrives wearing a fentanyl patch that contributes to baseline opioid exposure. Which perioperative decision must be made deliberately rather than allowing the patch to be managed by default?
options: Whether to apply a second patch
Whether to replace it automatically with an IV infusion
Whether to continue or remove it while maintaining appropriate baseline analgesia
Whether to cut the patch to reduce its dose
questions.explanation: A transdermal fentanyl patch may represent a substantial component of baseline opioid exposure, and heat, perfusion changes, or removal can alter delivery. The perioperative plan should explicitly decide whether it remains in place and how baseline opioid will be maintained if it is removed.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A physically opioid-dependent patient receives no baseline opioid on the day of surgery to 'avoid respiratory depression' and later develops tachycardia, diaphoresis, cramping, and agitation. Which management error MOST directly caused this?
options: Excessive continuation of the patient's usual opioid
Failure to use a mixed agonist-antagonist
Failure to provide adequate baseline opioid exposure to prevent withdrawal
questions.explanation: Avoiding all opioid in a physically dependent patient does not eliminate risk; it creates abrupt loss of baseline mu-receptor stimulation and can precipitate withdrawal. Baseline opioid should be maintained or equivalently replaced while additional analgesia is titrated safely.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A patient discloses daily oxycodone use only shortly before induction. What is the most important immediate response?
options: Clarify the drug, dose, timing, indication, tolerance/dependence, and last dose, then adapt the perioperative analgesic plan
Assume the history is too late to change management
Give a mixed agonist-antagonist to test for dependence
questions.explanation: Late discovery of daily oxycodone use should trigger rapid medication reconciliation: exact formulation, dose, schedule, indication, last dose, duration, tolerance/dependence, and other CNS depressants. That information determines withdrawal prevention, expected acute-pain requirements, and respiratory risk.
questions.topic: Dependence, tolerance, and the opioid-dependent patient

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic cancer has severe multifocal bone pain without a focal target for regional intervention. Which medication class remains the mainstay for severe cancer pain?
questions.explanation: Systemic opioids remain central for moderate-to-severe cancer pain because they can be titrated across diffuse or multifocal pain when no single regional target exists. Adjuvants, disease-directed treatment, and interventional techniques should be added according to mechanism and adverse effects.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: A patient with pancreatic cancer has severe visceral upper-abdominal pain despite systemic opioids and develops dose-limiting sedation. Which targeted intervention can reduce transmission through the visceral sympathetic pathway?
questions.explanation: Upper-abdominal visceral pain from pancreatic cancer is transmitted in part through sympathetic pathways associated with the celiac plexus. Celiac plexus block or neurolysis can reduce that nociceptive transmission and may lower systemic opioid requirements when sedation or other opioid toxicity becomes limiting.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: A patient with cancer pain remains severely symptomatic despite optimized systemic opioids and develops intolerable sedation and constipation with further escalation. Which escalation strategy is MOST appropriate to consider?
questions.explanation: Intrathecal drug delivery places analgesic near spinal receptors and can provide analgesia with lower systemic exposure in selected refractory cancer pain. It is considered when optimized systemic therapy is ineffective or causes unacceptable toxicity and requires appropriate procedural expertise and follow-up.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: Which drug classes manage most cancer pain? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Cancer pain often has mixed nociceptive and neuropathic mechanisms. Opioids remain central for severe nociceptive pain, while anticonvulsants and antidepressants can treat neuropathic components; the regimen should be individualized to pain mechanism and treatment goals.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: An older adult reports surprisingly little pain after hip-fracture repair but becomes distressed quickly once pain is established. Which age-related pattern BEST fits the source?
options: Higher pain threshold with lower pain tolerance
questions.explanation: Population studies of pain threshold and tolerance in older adults are variable and should not be treated as a fixed bedside rule. The clinically useful point is to assess each older patient directly because sensory changes, cognition, neuropathy, frailty, and pharmacologic sensitivity can alter both pain reporting and treatment response.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: An 85-year-old rates pain lower than expected but becomes distressed quickly once pain starts. How do pain threshold and tolerance change in older adults?
questions.explanation: Age-related pain research is heterogeneous, so a universal claim that every older adult has a higher threshold and lower tolerance should be applied cautiously. Individual assessment is more reliable because neuropathy, cognition, prior pain, mood, culture, and physiologic reserve vary widely.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: Which geriatric factors affect pain? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Peripheral neuropathy and age-related sensory changes can alter nociceptive input, while cognitive impairment can limit self-report and altered pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics can change treatment response. These factors make individualized geriatric pain assessment and dosing essential.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: A very preterm infant requires surgery. Which statement best reflects contemporary understanding of neonatal pain?
options: Pain pathways are absent until after birth
Pain perception begins only at term
Preterm infants can mount nociceptive responses and require appropriate analgesia; a single gestational-age cutoff should not be used to deny pain treatment
Analgesia is unnecessary before 28 weeks' gestation
questions.explanation: Preterm neonates have developing nociceptive pathways and demonstrate physiologic and behavioral responses to noxious stimulation. Exact developmental milestones are complex and should not be reduced to a single cutoff for whether an infant can experience or respond to pain.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: A 3-year-old cannot describe pain after a hernia repair. Which signs suggest pain? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Young children may communicate pain through facial expression, crying, guarding/body movement, sleep or activity change, and inability to be consoled. Age-appropriate validated behavioral tools should be used when reliable self-report is not possible.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: A 10-year-old undergoes the same procedure as an adult. Which principle should guide postoperative pain assessment?
options: Use heart rate alone because pediatric self-report is unreliable
Assume every child has a lower pain threshold than every adult
Assume children tolerate pain better than adults
Use an age-appropriate validated self-report or behavioral tool and treat the child's report individually rather than assuming a fixed pain threshold relative to adults
questions.explanation: Pain experience varies among individuals and across development. Children who can self-report should be assessed with age-appropriate validated tools; broad claims that all children have a uniformly lower or higher pain threshold than adults are not reliable for individual care.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: A child is calm in PACU until a visibly panicked parent arrives, after which crying and reported pain intensify. Which interpretation BEST supports family-centered pain care?
options: Parental distress can amplify the child's distress and should itself be addressed
Parental presence directly causes nociception and should always be prohibited
The child's pain report becomes invalid when a parent is anxious
Parental anxiety has no meaningful effect on pediatric distress
questions.explanation: A parent's visible distress can increase a child's fear and behavioral distress, which can intensify the pain experience or its expression. Family-centered care therefore includes supporting and coaching caregivers as part of the child's perioperative comfort plan.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: A child's parents are anxious and tearful in PACU. What approach is emphasized for pediatric pain?
options: Excluding parents from the recovery area
Family-centered care to reduce parental stress
questions.explanation: Family-centered pediatric pain care recognizes that caregiver anxiety and behavior influence the child's distress and coping. Clear information, reassurance, and involving parents appropriately can reduce distress while validated pain assessment and analgesic treatment continue.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: A stoic patient refuses analgesia, his family fears addiction, and a nurse doubts his pain. Which barriers are present? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Stoicism can suppress pain reporting, opiophobia can cause refusal because of addiction fears, and clinician bias can lead to undertreatment despite patient need. Identifying these barriers allows education and culturally responsive assessment rather than assuming low reported treatment demand means low pain.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: A surgical unit consistently undertreats pain because staff equate appropriate postoperative opioid use with addiction. Which intervention MOST directly addresses this barrier?
options: Use vital signs instead of patient reports
Targeted education correcting misconceptions about pain and opioid use
questions.explanation: When staff conflate appropriate short-term postoperative opioid treatment with addiction, education should distinguish expected analgesic use, tolerance, physical dependence, and opioid use disorder while reinforcing safe prescribing and monitoring. Correcting the misconception directly targets the identified barrier to treatment.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: Which system effects of poorly managed pain are shown on the consequences slide? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Poorly controlled pain can activate sympathetic cardiovascular responses, impair deep breathing and cough, slow gastrointestinal and urinary function, alter immune/endocrine responses, disturb sleep and mood, and delay mobilization. The consequences extend beyond discomfort and can interfere with recovery.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: A postoperative pathway treats effective pain control as a core recovery goal rather than an optional comfort measure. Which outcome rationale best supports that approach?
options: Analgesia removes the need for anesthetic drugs
Effective analgesia supports recovery outcomes and patient satisfaction
questions.explanation: Effective analgesia supports breathing, mobilization, sleep, participation in therapy, and patient experience while reducing excessive stress responses and rescue-treatment delays. Outcomes depend on balancing pain relief with adverse effects rather than pursuing a pain score of zero at any cost.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: An older patient reports severe pain despite receiving a dose that another older patient tolerated poorly. Which conclusion BEST reflects the geriatric evidence in the source?
options: Geriatric pain findings are variable, so assessment and dosing must be individualized
Age alone reliably predicts a lower analgesic requirement
Older adults consistently require higher opioid doses
Older adults experience little clinically important pain
questions.explanation: Older adults vary substantially in nociception, communication, cognition, comorbidity, and sensitivity to analgesics. A dose tolerated poorly by one patient should not be used to invalidate another patient's report; treatment should be titrated to that individual's pain, function, and adverse effects.
questions.topic: Cancer pain, geriatrics, pediatrics, and barriers

questions.stem: A 64-year-old is scheduled for an open thoracotomy. Which analgesic plan is BEST?
options: IV morphine PCA with a basal infusion and no adjuncts or regional blocks
Oral oxycodone started the morning after surgery on the floor
Intra-articular local anesthetic with ketorolac at incision
questions.explanation: Open thoracotomy produces severe dynamic pain that can impair ventilation and coughing. Thoracic epidural or paravertebral analgesia combined with multimodal systemic therapy can provide strong pain control and reduce opioid burden, with technique choice based on contraindications and patient-specific risk.

questions.stem: For a thoracotomy patient, why is regional analgesia emphasized beyond intraop use?
options: It replaces the need for incentive spirometry
It shortens the surgical procedure by relaxing chest wall muscles
It supports coughing and deep breathing to prevent pneumonia
questions.explanation: Thoracic pain causes splinting, shallow breathing, and ineffective cough, increasing atelectasis and pulmonary complication risk. Regional analgesia can improve dynamic pain enough to support deep breathing, coughing, mobilization, and pulmonary toilet.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with obstructive sleep apnea undergoes total knee arthroplasty. Which plan BEST balances strong analgesia with reduced opioid-related ventilatory risk?
options: Scheduled systemic opioids as the primary strategy without regional analgesia
High-dose IV hydromorphone with a routine basal PCA infusion
Intrathecal morphine plus a basal opioid PCA regardless of monitoring
Regional analgesia plus scheduled nonopioid multimodal therapy and limited rescue opioid
questions.explanation: OSA increases sensitivity to opioid-related ventilatory depression and upper-airway obstruction. Regional analgesia plus scheduled nonopioid multimodal therapy reduces opioid requirement, reserving carefully titrated systemic opioid for breakthrough pain while maintaining appropriate respiratory monitoring.

questions.stem: An ambulatory patient receives spinal anesthesia for knee arthroscopy and has prolonged motor block delaying discharge. What change would prevent this next time?
options: Lower local anesthetic dose with an intrathecal lipophilic opioid
Higher bupivacaine dose to shorten block duration
Intrathecal morphine to speed motor recovery
Epidural catheter instead of spinal for all ambulatory cases
questions.explanation: For short ambulatory procedures, excessive intrathecal local anesthetic can prolong motor recovery and delay walking or discharge. A smaller local-anesthetic dose supplemented by a lipophilic intrathecal opioid can preserve analgesia while reducing duration of motor block when clinically appropriate.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for an interscalene block asks why she should take her pain pills before the block wears off. What is the BEST explanation?
options: It prevents the block from lasting too long
It prevents sudden severe pain when the block resolves
It reduces the risk of local anesthetic toxicity
It is needed if pain is present at discharge
questions.explanation: The block may resolve faster than an oral rescue analgesic begins working. Taking the prescribed medication before sensory block resolution creates pharmacologic overlap and reduces the abrupt transition from near-complete regional analgesia to severe surgical pain.

questions.stem: A patient tells you she will refuse opioids after her hysterectomy because she fears addiction. What is the BEST response?
options: Prescribe opioids and let her decide later
Address her concerns and plan multimodal analgesia with education
Avoid all analgesics to respect her wishes
questions.explanation: Fear of addiction is a recognized barrier that should be addressed with accurate education and shared planning rather than dismissed. A multimodal plan can emphasize nonopioid and regional options while preserving carefully monitored opioid rescue if needed for function and humane pain control.

questions.stem: A patient received hydromorphone preoperatively and is drowsy but conversant. What determines whether she can provide valid consent?
options: Normal vital signs alone establish capacity
Any opioid exposure automatically invalidates consent
A family member can make her consent valid by co-signing
Whether she currently has decision-making capacity, including understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and ability to communicate a choice
questions.explanation: Medication exposure alone does not invalidate consent. Capacity depends on the patient's present ability to understand relevant information, appreciate how it applies personally, reason among options, and communicate a consistent choice; sedation or delirium matters only insofar as it impairs those abilities.

questions.stem: Fentanyl is given at induction, but positioning delays incision for 30 minutes. Hemodynamics rise sharply when incision finally occurs. Which planning error BEST explains the response?
options: The opioid's peak and useful duration were not matched to the timing of surgical stimulation
Fentanyl necessarily peaks 30 minutes after administration
The induction dose accumulated excessively before incision
Chest-wall rigidity is the expected cause of incision-related tachycardia
questions.explanation: Analgesic dosing should be synchronized with the expected noxious stimulus. A 30-minute delay can separate fentanyl's peak effect from incision, so failure to reassess and retitrate before the eventual incision leaves inadequate antinociception at the moment it is needed.

questions.stem: An obese, anxious patient receives a large opioid dose before preoxygenation, becomes somnolent and apneic, and fails to achieve an adequate end-tidal oxygen concentration. Which error MOST directly contributed?
options: Opioid peak effect was allowed to impair cooperation and ventilation during preoxygenation
The opioid dose was inadequate for preoxygenation
Nasal cannula oxygen would have eliminated opioid-induced apnea
questions.explanation: Preoxygenation depends on adequate ventilation and patient cooperation. A large opioid dose peaking before denitrogenation is complete can cause somnolence, hypoventilation, or apnea, preventing an adequate end-tidal oxygen concentration and reducing safe apnea time.

questions.stem: Near emergence, a spontaneously breathing patient is tachypneic with dilated pupils after a painful procedure. Which interpretation is best?
options: The findings prove inadequate analgesia and mandate an opioid bolus
Inadequate analgesia is possible, but these findings are nonspecific and should be integrated with ventilation, arousability, hemodynamics, temperature, and other causes before giving more opioid
The respiratory rate alone determines extubation readiness
questions.explanation: Tachypnea and dilated pupils can suggest pain or inadequate antinociception but are not specific. Near emergence, additional opioid should be based on the full picture including ventilation, arousability, hemodynamics, temperature, anxiety, residual stimulation, and other causes to avoid trading transient signs for post-extubation respiratory depression.

questions.stem: During emergence, a spontaneously breathing patient has RR 8/min with pinpoint pupils after repeated opioid doses, while quantitative neuromuscular recovery is adequate. Which cause is most likely?
questions.explanation: Bradypnea and pinpoint pupils after repeated opioid dosing are characteristic of excessive opioid effect, especially when quantitative neuromuscular recovery is adequate. Management should prioritize adequate ventilation and arousability and reduce or reverse opioid effect as clinically necessary.

questions.stem: After craniotomy, a patient coughs during emergence and transiently becomes hypertensive while ventilation remains adequate. Which intervention is MOST likely to create avoidable post-extubation hypoventilation?
options: Large opioid boluses given primarily to suppress the transient blood-pressure response
IV lidocaine used to blunt airway reflexes
questions.explanation: Coughing can transiently raise blood pressure during emergence, but a large opioid bolus may outlast that brief stimulus. Once the tube is removed, the residual opioid can depress ventilatory drive and worsen upper-airway obstruction, creating avoidable post-extubation hypoventilation.

questions.stem: An opioid-treated patient is hypoventilating, but severe surgical pain is expected immediately after extubation. What is the main danger of giving a large naloxone dose?
options: Abrupt reversal can produce severe pain while eliminating needed analgesia
Naloxone has no effect on postoperative pain
questions.explanation: Naloxone reverses opioid analgesia along with ventilatory depression. A large dose can abruptly produce severe pain and sympathetic activation, so when complete reversal is unnecessary it should be titrated to restore adequate ventilation while preserving as much analgesia as possible.

questions.stem: After laparoscopic colectomy, the team wants an adjunct that can reduce opioid exposure while also improving bowel recovery. Which infusion BEST fits both goals?
questions.explanation: IV lidocaine reduces opioid use, attenuates postoperative ileus, and speeds discharge after colectomy.

questions.stem: Perioperative magnesium is added to a multimodal spine-surgery plan. Which outcome would support its intended role?
options: Neuromuscular blockade as the primary analgesic mechanism
Predictable elimination of all postoperative pain
Reduced postoperative pain and/or opioid requirement
questions.explanation: Magnesium has been studied as an opioid-sparing adjunct and may reduce postoperative pain or opioid consumption. Regimens vary, and dosing should account for renal function, hemodynamics, and potentiation of neuromuscular blockade.

questions.stem: Subanesthetic ketamine is added to a painful spine case. Which therapeutic goal best matches this strategy?
options: Opioid-sparing analgesia and attenuation of central sensitization/hyperalgesia
questions.explanation: Subanesthetic ketamine provides analgesic and antihyperalgesic effects through NMDA-receptor antagonism and can reduce opioid requirements. Effective bolus and infusion regimens vary; no single dose pair is universally required.

questions.stem: A fentanyl infusion has run throughout a long operation and is stopped only at skin closure. The patient remains slow to emerge despite normal organ function. Which mechanism BEST explains this?
options: Prolongation of context-sensitive half-time from tissue accumulation and redistribution
Rapid redistribution from plasma into the brain after stopping the infusion
questions.explanation: Fentanyl accumulates in peripheral tissues during prolonged infusion and later redistributes into plasma after the infusion stops. This lengthens its context-sensitive half-time and can delay emergence even when organ function is normal.

questions.stem: A remifentanil infusion provides excellent intraoperative analgesia, but the patient awakens with immediate severe pain when it is discontinued. Which transition was missed?
options: Continue remifentanil routinely on the unmonitored ward
Establish longer-acting analgesia before remifentanil is stopped
Increase volatile anesthetic at closure to provide postoperative analgesia
questions.explanation: Remifentanil is hydrolyzed rapidly by nonspecific esterases, so its analgesic effect disappears within minutes of stopping even after a long infusion. Longer-acting systemic or regional analgesia should therefore be established before discontinuation when substantial postoperative pain is expected.

questions.stem: A patient reaches PACU with 9/10 pain, but no rescue analgesic is immediately available because postoperative orders are still pending. Which perioperative planning step would most directly have prevented this treatment gap?
options: Rely on intraoperative opioid to cover all PACU pain
Wait for the surgeon to enter orders after arrival
Ensure appropriate analgesics/orders are available for transport and handoff before leaving the OR
questions.explanation: Bringing medication to PACU prevents gaps in pain control during handoff.

questions.stem: A hydromorphone PCA order includes a 0.4-mg demand dose but accidentally omits the lockout interval. Why is this especially dangerous?
options: Repeated successful demands could rapidly deliver excessive opioid and cause respiratory depression
The patient will necessarily receive too little opioid
The pump cannot function without a basal rate
Patient control prevents overdose even without a lockout
questions.explanation: The PCA lockout limits how frequently another demand dose can be delivered. Omitting it removes a major programming safeguard and can permit rapid dose stacking, excessive sedation, and respiratory depression.

questions.stem: An opioid-naive patient is prescribed PCA after major surgery. Which order feature MOST unnecessarily increases respiratory risk?
questions.explanation: A basal infusion continues delivering opioid even after an opioid-naive patient becomes sedated and stops pressing the demand button. This removes the self-limiting feedback of demand-only PCA and increases respiratory-depression risk.

questions.stem: A PCA patient is difficult to arouse with a respiratory rate of 8/min. Which action has priority while the cause is addressed?
options: Increase the basal infusion to stabilize plasma concentration
Increase the demand dose because pain may cause somnolence
Stop further opioid delivery and support ventilation
Delay intervention until a formal pain score is obtained
questions.explanation: Difficulty arousing a PCA patient with bradypnea suggests clinically important opioid effect. Stop additional opioid delivery, support the airway and ventilation, assess oxygenation and ventilation, and use reversal when clinically indicated.

questions.stem: Four hours after intrathecal morphine, a patient has excellent analgesia, normal ventilation, and severe pruritus. Which treatment BEST preserves analgesia?
questions.explanation: Neuraxial opioid pruritus is largely centrally opioid-receptor mediated rather than a histamine allergy. Very low-dose naloxone can reduce itching while attempting to preserve analgesia; larger antagonistic doses are more likely to reverse pain relief.

questions.stem: Six hours after intrathecal morphine, a patient who was previously stable develops RR 6/min. Which mechanism best fits the timing?
options: Delayed respiratory depression from cephalad spread of hydrophilic morphine
questions.explanation: Intrathecal morphine is hydrophilic, remains in cerebrospinal fluid longer, and can spread rostrally over hours. This explains delayed respiratory depression after an initially stable period and the need for extended respiratory monitoring.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after intrathecal fentanyl, a patient develops RR 7/min. Which neuraxial-opioid pattern best fits this early event?
options: Delayed respiratory depression from hydrophilic morphine
Early respiratory depression from a lipophilic opioid
Delayed fentanyl effect occurring many hours later
questions.explanation: Lipophilic neuraxial opioids such as fentanyl enter spinal tissues and systemic circulation rapidly, so respiratory depression tends to occur earlier than with hydrophilic morphine. Bradypnea shortly after dosing fits this early pattern.

questions.stem: After midazolam and fentanyl sedation, a patient is drowsy and hypoventilating. What is the immediate priority?
options: Give enough naloxone to abolish all analgesia
Give flumazenil automatically before assessing the airway
Support airway and ventilation, stop contributing sedatives, and then selectively titrate drug-specific reversal when indicated
Wait for oxygen desaturation before intervening
questions.explanation: Ventilatory support is the first priority. Flumazenil or naloxone may be appropriate depending on the suspected contribution and patient-specific risks, but neither should replace immediate airway/ventilatory management or be used by a rigid sequence.

questions.stem: A patient remains deeply sedated after dexmedetomidine, with airway and hemodynamics currently supportable. Which pharmacologic limitation shapes management?
options: No routinely available human reversal agent exists
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine has no routinely used specific reversal drug in human perioperative practice. Management relies on reducing or stopping the infusion and supporting airway, ventilation, heart rate, and blood pressure as needed while the drug effect dissipates.

questions.stem: After several analgesic agents, a patient becomes hypotensive with sinus tachycardia. Which response BEST avoids treating a number without identifying the cause?
options: Assess volume status and hemodynamics, then give fluid or vasopressor as indicated
Give more opioid because tachycardia proves pain
Give flumazenil regardless of medications received
questions.explanation: Tachycardic hypotension after analgesic therapy can reflect hypovolemia, vasodilation, bleeding, or other causes. Assess perfusion and volume status first, then use fluid, vasopressor, or other targeted therapy according to the mechanism.

questions.stem: During a dexmedetomidine infusion, HR is 38/min and BP is 80/40 mm Hg. Besides reducing or stopping the infusion, which approach is most appropriate?
options: Glycopyrrolate is mandatory in every case
Treat symptomatic bradycardia and hypotension according to mechanism and severity with appropriate chronotropic and/or vasopressor support
Naloxone is the specific dexmedetomidine antidote
Observe without treatment because dexmedetomidine bradycardia is always benign
questions.explanation: Severe bradycardia with hypotension requires prompt hemodynamic support. Depending on the clinical situation, anticholinergic therapy, ephedrine, epinephrine, fluids, or other vasopressor/chronotropic treatment may be appropriate; there is no single mandatory drug.

questions.stem: A patient has good opioid analgesia but develops nausea without respiratory depression or other toxicity. Which intervention best treats the adverse effect while preserving analgesia?
questions.explanation: Opioid nausea usually responds to antiemetics.

questions.stem: A patient lists 'morphine allergy' because prior morphine caused isolated itching without swelling, bronchospasm, or hypotension. What is the BEST next step?
options: Treat the history as prior anaphylaxis
Label all opioids as absolutely contraindicated
Administer prophylactic epinephrine before any analgesic
Clarify and document the reaction because isolated pruritus is commonly an opioid adverse effect
questions.explanation: Isolated opioid-associated itching is a common adverse effect and may reflect central mu-receptor effects or histamine release rather than true allergy. Clarifying the exact reaction prevents an inaccurate allergy label from unnecessarily restricting future analgesic choices.

questions.stem: A regional block has already delivered bupivacaine, and the surgeon plans a large additional bupivacaine infiltration at closure. What should determine whether the infiltration proceeds?
options: The cumulative dose from every source relative to the patient's safe weight-based limit
Only the surgeon's infiltration dose because block doses are counted separately
The tissue plane, because subcutaneous dosing cannot cause systemic toxicity
Whether the injections are separated by different clinicians
questions.explanation: Local-anesthetic toxicity risk reflects cumulative systemic exposure, so bupivacaine administered in the block and by surgical infiltration must be totaled. The additional dose should proceed only if cumulative exposure and patient-specific risk remain acceptable.

questions.stem: A block is planned in a remote clinic without lipid emulsion. What is the BEST decision?
options: Proceed and call for lipids from the main OR if needed
Do not proceed until emergency equipment is available
questions.explanation: Regional anesthesia can produce complications requiring immediate recognition and treatment. A site without appropriate monitoring, airway/resuscitation equipment, and lipid emulsion is not an appropriate environment until those resources are available.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic back pain takes oxycodone 30 mg daily. What should be done on the day of surgery?
options: Skip the dose to reduce respiratory risk
Take the usual dose or give an equivalent preop dose
questions.explanation: Chronic daily opioid exposure may produce physical dependence, and abrupt omission can precipitate withdrawal while worsening perioperative pain. Baseline opioid exposure should generally be continued or appropriately replaced, with additional surgical analgesia managed separately.

questions.stem: A patient maintained on buprenorphine 16 mg/day for opioid use disorder requires ankle ORIF. Which perioperative strategy BEST maintains treatment while addressing surgical pain?
options: Avoid all opioid analgesia regardless of pain severity
Continue buprenorphine and use multimodal therapy with supplemental full agonists when needed
questions.explanation: Current perioperative strategies commonly favor continuing buprenorphine for opioid use disorder rather than routinely stopping it. Multimodal and regional analgesia should be maximized, with supplemental full agonists titrated when needed for additional acute pain.

questions.stem: An opioid-dependent patient receives butorphanol and shortly develops tachycardia, diaphoresis, cramping, and agitation. Which receptor-level effect BEST explains the event?
options: A mixed agonist-antagonist displaced full mu agonist effect and precipitated withdrawal
Butorphanol's serotonin reuptake inhibition caused serotonin syndrome
Excess kappa antagonism produced respiratory depression
questions.explanation: Butorphanol's mixed agonist-antagonist activity can reduce effective mu-receptor stimulation in a patient dependent on a full mu agonist. That abrupt receptor-level change can precipitate autonomic and gastrointestinal withdrawal.

questions.stem: A patient with long-term high-dose opioid therapy reports worsening diffuse pain as opioid doses rise, without a new surgical complication. Which phenomenon should enter the differential?
questions.explanation: Paradoxically increasing diffuse pain with escalating opioid exposure can suggest opioid-induced hyperalgesia, although tolerance and disease progression must also be considered. Management emphasizes reassessment and multimodal strategies rather than reflexive escalation of the same opioid.

questions.stem: A patient taking 120 mg oral morphine equivalents daily needs PCA after laminectomy. Which feature may be reasonable specifically because substantial baseline opioid tolerance already exists?
options: A fixed 60-minute lockout regardless of analgesic response
A carefully calculated basal infusion in addition to demand dosing
questions.explanation: A basal PCA infusion can be considered in selected opioid-tolerant patients when it replaces part of a known baseline opioid requirement. It should be derived conservatively from actual prior exposure and paired with close reassessment.

questions.stem: Which FOUR strategies can be useful components of perioperative analgesia for an opioid-tolerant patient? (Select 4)
options: Nonopioid multimodal analgesics selected for patient risk
Individualized continuation/replacement of baseline opioid with carefully titrated supplemental opioid
Mandatory high-dose gabapentinoids for every patient
questions.explanation: Opioid-tolerant patients benefit from maintaining baseline opioid exposure, individualized supplemental opioid, and multimodal/regional strategies when appropriate. No single adjunct, including a high-dose gabapentinoid, is mandatory for every patient.

questions.stem: A patient with a fentanyl patch is scheduled for surgery. What should be considered?
options: Replace the patch with a naloxone infusion during surgery
Remove the patch and give IV fentanyl
Whether to keep or remove the patch based on the plan
questions.explanation: A fentanyl patch may provide a major portion of baseline opioid exposure, while heat, perfusion, or removal can change drug delivery. The perioperative plan should explicitly decide whether to continue it and how baseline opioid will be replaced if removed.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic cancer has intolerable sedation and constipation from high-dose oral opioids. Which option can help?
options: Stopping opioids and using NSAIDs alone
Increasing the oral opioid dose further
questions.explanation: Intrathecal drug delivery can provide spinal analgesia with lower systemic drug exposure in selected patients whose cancer pain remains refractory or whose systemic adverse effects are unacceptable. It is an escalation strategy requiring procedural expertise and follow-up.

questions.stem: A patient with pancreatic cancer has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back despite high-dose opioids. Which intervention helps?
options: TAP block with a continuous catheter infusion
