questions.explanation: Preventive analgesia requires more than preincisional timing. The technique should suppress clinically important nociceptive input with sufficient intensity, cover the relevant surgical field, and persist while substantial postoperative input continues.

questions.stem: An older adult with mild cognitive impairment becomes intermittently confused after repeated opioid doses. Which age-related concern should MOST influence further treatment?
options: Faster drug metabolism shortens every opioid effect
Older age reliably produces opioid tolerance
Higher pain tolerance requires larger routine opioid doses
Greater vulnerability to oversedation and delirium requires cautious titration and reassessment
questions.explanation: Older adults may have altered pharmacokinetics, reduced physiologic reserve, and greater susceptibility to opioid-related sedation and delirium. New confusion after repeated doses should prompt dose reduction and reassessment rather than assuming undertreated pain.

questions.stem: Case R: A 68-year-old has mild cognitive impairment and is receiving opioids. What approach is BEST?
options: Lower doses, careful titration, and multimodal adjuncts
Standard adult doses, since pain threshold rises with age
questions.explanation: In an older adult with cognitive vulnerability, use smaller individualized doses, titrate to function and observed response, and use opioid-sparing multimodal strategies when appropriate. Frequent reassessment is more reliable than a fixed age-based dose reduction.

questions.stem: A patient taking an SSRI becomes agitated and tachycardic after tramadol. Which pharmacologic property makes this combination concerning?
options: Tramadol is a pure mu agonist with no monoamine effect
Tramadol has serotonergic/norepinephrine reuptake effects in addition to opioid activity
Tramadol directly antagonizes SSRIs and precipitates opioid withdrawal
Tramadol is a local anesthetic that causes systemic toxicity
questions.explanation: Tramadol inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake in addition to weak mu-opioid activity. Combining it with an SSRI increases serotonergic toxicity risk, making agitation and autonomic activation concerning.

questions.stem: Case S: The patient on an SSRI developed agitation and tachycardia after tramadol. What lesson applies to tramadol?
options: It is a pure mu agonist with no monoamine activity
It is safe with all antidepressants
questions.explanation: Tramadol is pharmacologically complex because it has serotonergic and noradrenergic activity, depends partly on CYP2D6 for an active opioid metabolite, and interacts with multiple CNS medications. It should not be treated as a simple interchangeable opioid.

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient arrives for surgery with a PCA already in use. Before adding anesthetic opioids, which information is MOST important?
options: Only the programmed settings, regardless of doses actually received
Recent delivered doses and timing, along with the current PCA regimen
questions.explanation: Recent PCA delivery determines the patient's current opioid burden. Knowing the drug, concentration, basal rate if present, demand dose, successful doses, last delivery, and clinical response helps prevent additive oversedation or inadvertent loss of baseline therapy.

questions.stem: Case T: A patient with chronic pain arrives on a PCA. What is the risk of ignoring prior PCA dosing?
options: Oversedation or withdrawal due to mismatched dosing
No change in outcomes, since the OR plan overrides PCA
questions.explanation: Ignoring prior PCA exposure can lead to excessive supplemental dosing if substantial opioid was recently delivered, or withdrawal and undertreatment if chronic baseline therapy is interrupted. Medication reconciliation must precede new dosing.

questions.stem: After laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a patient has shoulder-tip pain without shoulder injury. Which mechanism BEST explains the symptom?
options: Superficial somatic pain from shoulder skin
Referred visceral pain from diaphragmatic/peritoneal irritation
Peripheral neuropathy from surgical transection at the shoulder
Deep somatic pain from bone injury
questions.explanation: Pneumoperitoneum can irritate the diaphragm and adjacent peritoneum, with afferent convergence producing pain perceived at the shoulder rather than the abdomen. This is a classic referred visceral pain pattern.

questions.stem: Case U: A patient undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy and has referred shoulder pain. Which intervention may help?
options: Stop all analgesics until the pain localizes
questions.explanation: Nonpharmacologic interventions and multimodal analgesia help.

questions.stem: Soon after neuraxial fentanyl, a patient develops clinically significant hypoventilation. Which response has priority?
options: Give flumazenil as the opioid antagonist
Wait because only delayed respiratory depression is clinically important
Administer more fentanyl to prevent withdrawal
Support ventilation and titrate naloxone if opioid reversal is required
questions.explanation: Clinically significant hypoventilation after neuraxial fentanyl is an airway and ventilation problem first. Support ventilation, stop further depressant dosing, and titrate naloxone when opioid antagonism is needed.

questions.stem: Clinically significant respiratory depression occurs soon after neuraxial fentanyl. Which property explains why the effect tends to appear early rather than many hours later?
options: High lipophilicity promotes rapid tissue/systemic uptake
Hydrophilicity promotes slow cephalad CSF spread
Slow metabolism creates delayed rostral migration
questions.explanation: Fentanyl is highly lipophilic, producing rapid spinal tissue uptake and systemic absorption after neuraxial administration. Its respiratory effects therefore tend to occur earlier than the delayed rostral-spread pattern of hydrophilic morphine.

questions.stem: Case W: A patient has pain and hypertension after a tourniquet. What should you do first?
options: Assess for tourniquet pain and treat appropriately
Increase fluids, since hypertension reflects hypovolemia
Treat as expected hypertension and continue
questions.explanation: Assess pain source; tourniquet pain is common.

questions.stem: A patient with tourniquet discomfort becomes hypertensive but is also newly hypoxemic. Which problem takes priority before escalating analgesia?
options: Give NSAID first because it cannot affect ventilation
Give opioid first because hypertension proves pain is primary
Treat the blood pressure without addressing oxygenation
questions.explanation: New hypoxemia can itself cause agitation and distress and represents an immediate physiologic threat. Oxygenation and ventilation should be corrected and the cause investigated before hypertension is attributed solely to tourniquet pain.

questions.stem: A patient maintained on methadone has an unexpectedly variable response to perioperative dosing despite adherence. Which property of methadone most complicates prediction of dose and effect?
options: Absence of clinically important drug interactions
Wide interpatient variability in pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and elimination half-life
questions.explanation: Methadone has substantial interpatient variability in metabolism, effect, and elimination half-life, with important drug interactions. Its behavior should not be reduced to a single CYP2D6 or genetic explanation.

questions.stem: A patient maintained on methadone presents for a painful operation. Which strategy BEST separates maintenance therapy from the additional surgical analgesic requirement?
options: Continue baseline methadone and add individualized multimodal perioperative analgesia
Stop all opioids until postoperative pain is measurable
Use acetaminophen alone because maintenance methadone covers surgical pain
questions.explanation: Maintenance methadone covers the patient's baseline opioid requirement and helps prevent withdrawal, but it does not automatically provide adequate analgesia for a new painful operation. Continue baseline therapy and add individualized procedure-specific multimodal analgesia.

questions.stem: A patient reports a 'morphine allergy' consisting only of prior generalized itching without swelling, bronchospasm, or hypotension. Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Clarify and document the reaction as a likely opioid adverse effect rather than automatically labeling anaphylaxis
Treat the historical event as active anaphylaxis
Give prophylactic epinephrine before any opioid
questions.explanation: Isolated opioid-associated pruritus is commonly a pharmacologic adverse effect or non-IgE-mediated histamine-related reaction rather than IgE-mediated anaphylaxis. The exact historical features should be clarified and documented.

questions.stem: A patient previously labeled 'morphine allergic' now reports that the historical reaction included facial swelling rather than isolated itching. How should this new information change the assessment?
options: It confirms a routine opioid adverse effect only
It raises concern for a potentially serious hypersensitivity reaction and warrants further evaluation
questions.explanation: Facial swelling/angioedema is more concerning than isolated pruritus and warrants careful evaluation of the original reaction and alternatives. It raises concern for serious hypersensitivity but does not by itself prove an IgE-mediated opioid allergy.

questions.stem: A PACU patient reports pain 8/10 but repeatedly falls asleep and has a respiratory rate of 8/min after opioid therapy. Which action BEST balances the pain report with immediate safety?
options: Ignore the pain score because sleeping proves the patient is comfortable
Give a large opioid bolus because self-reported pain always overrides sedation
Administer naloxone automatically without assessing ventilation
Reassess arousal and ventilation and withhold further opioid until respiratory safety is established
questions.explanation: A high pain score does not justify additional opioid when the patient is already difficult to keep awake and bradypneic. Immediate safety requires reassessing airway, ventilation, gas exchange, and sedation and withholding further opioid until respiratory stability is established.

questions.stem: Case Z: A patient in PACU has pain and a pain score of 8, but is sleeping and RR 8. What does this scenario illustrate?
options: Pain scores are accurate even when asleep
questions.explanation: Pain treatment is iterative rather than dose-and-forget. Repeated assessment of pain, function, arousability, respiratory status, and adverse effects is necessary because severe pain can coexist with unsafe opioid effect.

questions.stem: A severely anxious PACU patient hyperventilates and reports 10/10 pain despite substantial opioid already producing adequate analgesic exposure. Which next step BEST avoids compounding opioid toxicity?
options: Continue escalating opioid until the patient sleeps
Address anxiety with reassurance and an appropriate nonopioid/anxiolytic strategy while reassessing pain
Withhold all treatment because anxiety invalidates the pain report
Remove monitoring to reduce environmental stimulation
questions.explanation: Anxiety can magnify distress and pain reporting, while additional opioid in a patient with substantial existing exposure may add toxicity without addressing the dominant problem. Reassurance and carefully selected nonopioid or anxiolytic strategies should accompany reassessment.

questions.stem: Despite a structured multimodal plan, a high-risk patient continues to have difficult-to-control pain with complex chronic opioid exposure. Which systems resource should be available?
questions.explanation: High-risk chronic opioid exposure with persistent uncontrolled pain benefits from specialist input because management may require complex opioid conversion, maintenance therapy, regional techniques, neuropathic agents, and discharge planning.

questions.stem: An epidural that had provided good analgesia stops functioning and breakthrough pain develops. Which next step BEST avoids compounding toxicity from a rescue modality?
options: Give naloxone before troubleshooting the epidural
Increase every epidural medication without checking the catheter or block
Stop all analgesia to determine the true pain score
Reassess the epidural and patient, then add or change therapy with attention to overlapping effects
questions.explanation: Sudden breakthrough pain after a previously effective epidural may reflect catheter migration, disconnection, pump failure, inadequate spread, or a new complication. Troubleshooting the primary technique before indiscriminately adding systemic rescue therapy reduces overlapping toxicity.

questions.stem: A patient becomes apneic after receiving both opioid and benzodiazepine. Which intervention takes priority before deciding which reversal drug to use?
questions.explanation: Apnea after sedative and opioid administration requires immediate airway opening and ventilatory support regardless of which drug is responsible. Drug-specific antagonists may then be selected according to the suspected residual effect and patient-specific risks.

questions.stem: During an IV lidocaine infusion, a patient reports new circumoral numbness and metallic taste. Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Suspect early local-anesthetic systemic toxicity, stop the infusion, and assess immediately
Continue because these are expected analgesic endpoints
Treat empirically for hypocalcemia without changing lidocaine
questions.explanation: Circumoral numbness and metallic taste are classic early neurologic symptoms of local-anesthetic systemic toxicity. Stop lidocaine immediately, assess the patient, and prepare for escalation according to a LAST protocol if symptoms progress.

questions.stem: A peripheral nerve block is proposed in a room without immediate airway/resuscitation equipment or lipid emulsion. Which safety concern should determine whether to proceed?
options: Emergency equipment is unnecessary for ultrasound-guided blocks
Remote placement reduces complications because there are fewer interruptions
A serious block complication could occur before rescue resources arrive
Lowering the local-anesthetic dose eliminates the need for rescue capability
questions.explanation: Peripheral nerve blocks can cause complications that deteriorate rapidly. Appropriate monitoring, resuscitation equipment, and lipid emulsion must be immediately available rather than located elsewhere where treatment would be delayed.

questions.stem: During a low-dose ketamine infusion, a patient remains hemodynamically stable but develops vivid dreams and perceptual disturbances. Which drug effect best explains the symptoms?
questions.explanation: Ketamine can produce dissociation, vivid dreams, hallucinations, and other psychomimetic effects even at subanesthetic doses. Stable ventilation and hemodynamics with perceptual disturbance support this drug effect.

questions.stem: During a magnesium analgesic infusion, a patient shows greater-than-expected weakness after a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Which interaction should be suspected?
options: Acute opioid tolerance caused by magnesium
questions.explanation: Magnesium reduces acetylcholine release and decreases neuromuscular excitability, which can potentiate nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade. Unexpected weakness should therefore prompt quantitative neuromuscular assessment and adjustment of blocker or reversal strategy.

questions.stem: A patient wearing a transdermal fentanyl patch is placed under an active warming device during a long operation. Which pharmacokinetic concern is MOST important?
options: Heat can increase transdermal fentanyl absorption and opioid exposure
questions.explanation: Transdermal fentanyl delivery increases with skin temperature and local blood flow. Active warming over or near a patch can therefore increase systemic fentanyl exposure and raise the risk of excessive sedation and respiratory depression.

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient with severe anxiety and PTSD is scheduled for major surgery. Why should these comorbidities be addressed in the perioperative pain plan?
options: Opioids alone reliably treat both chronic pain and PTSD
Psychiatric symptoms should be deferred until surgical pain resolves
Psychological comorbidity can amplify pain experience and complicate analgesic management
Regional techniques are contraindicated when anxiety is present
questions.explanation: Anxiety and PTSD can heighten threat perception, sleep disturbance, autonomic arousal, and pain-related distress, complicating perioperative analgesia. Addressing these comorbidities with trauma-informed communication and individualized multimodal planning can improve pain management without assuming the pain is purely psychological.

questions.stem: After spine surgery, a patient describes burning pain radiating down the leg with electric shocks and allodynia. Which mechanism should be specifically targeted in addition to routine incisional analgesia?
questions.explanation: Burning, electric, radiating pain with allodynia indicates a neuropathic component from somatosensory nerve injury or dysfunction. That mechanism may require targeted adjuvants in addition to treatment of ordinary nociceptive incisional pain.

questions.stem: A postoperative patient reports that pain is tolerable at rest but becomes severe with coughing. In a structured pain history, how should coughing be classified?
questions.explanation: Coughing makes the patient's pain worse, so it is an exacerbating or provoking factor in the pain history. Identifying such factors also reveals dynamic pain that may interfere with pulmonary toilet or function despite acceptable resting pain.

questions.stem: A patient reports that applying ice consistently decreases incisional pain. In a structured pain assessment, what does this identify?
questions.explanation: Ice consistently reducing pain identifies a relieving or palliating factor. Recording what improves pain helps characterize the syndrome and identifies useful nonpharmacologic components of the treatment plan.

questions.stem: A patient says postoperative pain prevents walking to the bathroom despite tolerable pain at rest. Which assessment domain is most directly affected?
options: Interference with function and activities of daily living
questions.explanation: Pain that prevents walking is impairing function and activities of daily living even if resting intensity is tolerable. Functional assessment is essential because recovery goals depend on mobility and participation, not the resting numeric score alone.

questions.stem: After hernia repair, a patient is diaphoretic and nauseated but reports pain 2/10. Which interpretation BEST avoids unnecessary opioid administration?
options: Nausea is the most specific physiologic measure of postoperative pain
Sweating and nausea prove severe pain despite the patient's report
Patient self-report should be ignored when autonomic signs are present
Autonomic and gastrointestinal signs are nonspecific and may have causes other than pain
questions.explanation: Diaphoresis and nausea can accompany pain but are nonspecific and may reflect PONV, medication effects, hypoglycemia, hemodynamic changes, or other causes. A reliable low self-reported pain score should not be overridden solely by autonomic signs.

questions.stem: A unit routinely substitutes clinicians' visual estimates for patient-reported pain scores. Which error is MOST likely?
options: Systematic observer bias related to experience and assumptions
More accurate assessment than patient self-report
Elimination of cultural influences on pain assessment
questions.explanation: Clinician appearance-based estimates can under- or overestimate pain because behavior is influenced by culture, coping, prior experience, and observer assumptions. Reliable patient self-report should remain central, supplemented by function and clinical context.

questions.stem: A patient's pain management plan is agreed on by patient, surgeon, and anesthesia. Which note principle is this?
options: Plan developed in the PACU after emergence
questions.explanation: A perioperative pain plan is strongest when goals, expected techniques, rescue options, and patient preferences are discussed and aligned among the patient and relevant procedural and anesthesia teams before surgery. Shared planning reduces conflicting expectations and reactive treatment.

questions.stem: A thoracic epidural will require a higher-acuity postoperative location and specialized follow-up. When should these resources be secured?
options: Only after the first breakthrough-pain episode
After PACU arrival if the epidural still works
Before surgery as part of the analgesic plan
questions.explanation: A thoracic epidural may require specialized monitoring, staffing, anticoagulation coordination, and a particular postoperative unit. Those resources should be secured before surgery so disposition does not force unsafe monitoring or abandonment of the planned technique.

questions.stem: A patient receiving repeated opioids develops constipation without signs of withdrawal or another acute abdominal process. How should this finding be classified?
questions.explanation: Constipation is a common dose-related opioid adverse effect caused by reduced gastrointestinal motility and secretion. It should be anticipated and managed, especially with ongoing opioid therapy, rather than interpreted as evidence of withdrawal.

questions.stem: A patient has anaphylaxis after an analgesic. Which category is this?
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a listed adverse effect.

questions.stem: After neuraxial and systemic opioid exposure, a patient develops suprapubic fullness and inability to void. Which response best addresses this recognized opioid adverse effect?
options: Ignore it because retention is always self-limited
Assess bladder volume and manage urinary retention
questions.explanation: Opioids, including neuraxial opioids, can impair bladder emptying and cause urinary retention. Suprapubic fullness and inability to void warrant bladder-volume assessment and appropriate decompression or other management rather than additional analgesic escalation.

questions.stem: After colectomy, morphine monotherapy controls pain poorly and causes severe nausea and constipation. Which change BEST improves the therapeutic balance?
options: Stop antiemetics so nausea can guide opioid titration
Increase morphine and add a basal PCA infusion
Add nonopioid and/or regional multimodal strategies to reduce opioid requirement
Avoid all nonopioid agents to prevent drug interactions
questions.explanation: When opioid monotherapy causes nausea and constipation before adequate analgesia is achieved, adding therapies with different mechanisms can improve the therapeutic ratio. Nonopioid and regional techniques can reduce the opioid dose needed for comparable or better pain control.

questions.stem: A patient's pain is controlled with acetaminophen and NSAIDs. What does this demonstrate?
options: Higher respiratory depression risk from the combination
Improved analgesia and reduced opioid consumption
questions.explanation: Acetaminophen and NSAIDs act through complementary nonopioid mechanisms and can provide better analgesia together than either alone, reducing rescue opioid consumption. Their successful use demonstrates the opioid-sparing principle of multimodal analgesia.

questions.stem: A patient with significant renal impairment is receiving ketorolac as part of a multimodal regimen. Which adjustment is MOST appropriate?
options: Reconsider the NSAID and use renal-appropriate multimodal alternatives
Increase ketorolac because renal impairment reduces its effect
Continue the standard regimen without reassessment
Add morphine specifically to protect renal function
questions.explanation: NSAIDs can worsen renal perfusion and kidney injury in susceptible patients, so significant renal impairment changes their risk-benefit profile. Use renal-appropriate nonopioid or regional alternatives and individualize any opioid according to clearance and active metabolites.

questions.stem: A 75-kg patient has received no other local anesthetic. The surgeon requests 30 mL of 1% plain lidocaine. Using a maximum of about 4.5 mg/kg, which assessment is correct?
options: 300 mg exceeds a calculated 225 mg limit
300 mg is below the calculated ~337.5 mg limit, but cumulative dosing must still be tracked
questions.explanation: Thirty milliliters of 1% lidocaine contains 300 mg because 1% equals 10 mg/mL. The stated 4.5 mg/kg ceiling for 75 kg is 337.5 mg, so 300 mg is below that calculated value only if cumulative exposure and other LAST risk factors remain acceptable.

questions.stem: A patient receives 20 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine for an interscalene block, then the surgeon requests another 20 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine for infiltration. What cumulative dose must be evaluated against the patient's safe limit?
questions.explanation: A 0.5% solution contains 5 mg/mL. Forty total milliliters therefore equals 200 mg ropivacaine; the block and surgeon infiltration must be counted together when evaluating cumulative toxicity risk.

questions.stem: A protocol uses ketamine 0.2 mg/kg then 0.15 mg/kg/hr and magnesium 50 mg/kg then 8 mg/kg/hr. For a 60 kg patient, which set of calculated doses is correct?
options: Ketamine 12 mg then 90 mg/hr; magnesium 300 mg then 48 mg/hr
Ketamine 6 mg then 4.5 mg/hr; magnesium 1.5 g then 240 mg/hr
Ketamine 24 mg then 18 mg/hr; magnesium 6 g then 960 mg/hr
Ketamine 12 mg then 9 mg/hr; magnesium 3 g then 480 mg/hr
questions.explanation: Using the stated protocol: ketamine 0.2 × 60 = 12 mg and 0.15 × 60 = 9 mg/hr; magnesium 50 × 60 = 3,000 mg and 8 × 60 = 480 mg/hr. These are calculations, not universal dosing recommendations.

questions.stem: A PACU patient becomes somnolent with RR 6/min after hydromorphone and midazolam. Which principle best guides immediate management?
options: Support airway and ventilation first, then selectively titrate drug-specific reversal according to the suspected residual effects and patient-specific risks
Flumazenil must always be given before naloxone
Give a large naloxone dose before supporting ventilation
questions.explanation: Airway and ventilation are the immediate priorities. Naloxone and flumazenil can be used selectively when indicated, but there is no universal requirement to reverse the benzodiazepine first; flumazenil itself has important contraindications and seizure risk.

questions.stem: During emergence after laparotomy, an intubated patient is coughing, hypertensive, has dilated pupils, and breathes 26/min with adequate neuromuscular recovery. Which response BEST balances analgesia with extubation safety?
options: Give a large opioid bolus solely to normalize blood pressure
Carefully titrate opioid while reassessing ventilation and extubation readiness rather than treating blood pressure alone
Deepen volatile anesthesia and extubate regardless of readiness
questions.explanation: Coughing, hypertension, tachypnea, and mydriasis can accompany inadequate analgesia but are nonspecific. Near extubation, short-acting analgesia should be titrated cautiously while ventilation, arousability, anesthetic depth, and extubation readiness are reassessed so treatment does not create post-extubation hypoventilation.

questions.stem: A femoral nerve catheter provides excellent resting analgesia, but knee pain prevents participation in physical therapy. Which conclusion BEST guides adjustment of the plan?
options: Movement-related pain should not influence postoperative analgesia
The block is adequate because resting pain is controlled
Analgesic success should include functional pain with movement, not resting pain alone
The catheter should be removed because any movement pain proves block toxicity
questions.explanation: Excellent resting analgesia does not meet the recovery goal if pain prevents physical therapy. Regional and systemic analgesic plans should be assessed during movement and function, with adjustments that also preserve motor strength and safety.

questions.stem: A patient reports pain 9/10 while HR is 72/min and BP is 118/70 mm Hg. Which principle should govern the assessment?
options: Blood pressure is more reliable than self-report
Normal vital signs prove the pain is exaggerated
Analgesia should wait until sympathetic signs develop
Normal vital signs do not exclude severe pain; the patient's report remains central
questions.explanation: Normal heart rate and blood pressure do not exclude severe pain because physiologic responses are variable and nonspecific. When communication is reliable, the patient's validated self-report remains central and is integrated with function, sedation, and clinical context.

questions.stem: Which patient combines both a procedure strongly associated with chronic postsurgical pain and a modifiable perioperative risk factor?
options: A thoracotomy patient with severe poorly controlled acute postoperative pain
A laparoscopic appendectomy patient with effective analgesia
A cataract patient with minimal discomfort
A carpal-tunnel patient with well-controlled pain
questions.explanation: Thoracotomy is associated with persistent postsurgical pain, and severe poorly controlled acute postoperative pain is a potentially modifiable risk factor associated with chronicity. Strong acute pain management is therefore important, although it cannot guarantee prevention of chronic pain.

questions.stem: A patient maintained on buprenorphine has severe postoperative pain despite nonopioid adjuncts. Which strategy BEST avoids precipitating withdrawal while treating the new pain burden?
options: Continue buprenorphine and add appropriate full-mu agonist and multimodal therapy as needed
questions.explanation: Continuing buprenorphine helps maintain treatment stability and avoid abrupt loss of baseline opioid effect. Severe new surgical pain can be treated with multimodal and regional strategies plus appropriately titrated full mu agonists when needed rather than automatically discontinuing buprenorphine.

questions.stem: A physically opioid-dependent patient with only mild sedation receives a large naloxone dose and becomes acutely agitated, hypertensive, and tachycardic. Which error MOST directly caused the deterioration?
options: Excessive antagonist dosing precipitated withdrawal; naloxone should be titrated to the minimum effect needed
questions.explanation: A large naloxone dose can abruptly remove mu-receptor stimulation in a physically dependent patient, precipitating acute withdrawal and sympathetic activation. When full immediate reversal is unnecessary, naloxone should be titrated to the minimum amount needed to restore adequate ventilation.

questions.stem: A short procedure is induced with a large fentanyl bolus, and the patient remains slow to emerge after the surgery ends quickly. Which planning principle was missed?
options: Prefer long-acting opioids for all short procedures
Use additional opioid at emergence to accelerate redistribution
Match opioid onset, peak, and duration to the intensity and length of surgical stimulation
questions.explanation: A large fentanyl bolus can outlast a short procedure and delay recovery. Analgesic selection and timing should match the expected intensity and duration of stimulation, with shorter-acting or smaller titrated dosing when surgical duration is brief.

questions.stem: Ketorolac is given early during a vascular procedure before bleeding risk and surgical hemostasis are clarified. Which planning principle was missed?
options: Coordinate NSAID timing with the surgeon and bleeding context, often near the end of the case
NSAIDs should always be given at induction
NSAID timing is unrelated to surgical bleeding considerations
NSAIDs should replace all opioid therapy
questions.explanation: NSAID timing should reflect renal risk, procedure-specific bleeding consequences, and the state of surgical hemostasis. Giving ketorolac before those factors are clarified bypasses team-based risk assessment; there is no universal rule that every NSAID must wait until closure.

questions.stem: As closure begins after laparoscopic hernia repair, the planned local infiltration has not yet been performed and the cumulative local-anesthetic dose remains acceptable. Which action best preserves the multimodal plan?
options: Replace the infiltration automatically with extra IV opioid
Prompt the surgeon to perform the planned infiltration before emergence
Wait until severe PACU pain develops
Omit local anesthetic because closure has started
questions.explanation: Local infiltration before emergence targets incisional nociception and can reduce early rescue opioid need. If it remains part of the plan and cumulative local-anesthetic exposure is acceptable, prompting the surgeon before closure preserves that multimodal component.

questions.stem: A patient is receiving dexmedetomidine and hydromorphone and becomes excessively sedated. Which reversal is possible?
questions.explanation: Naloxone can antagonize hydromorphone's mu-opioid effects, but dexmedetomidine has no routinely available specific human reversal agent. Management of combined oversedation therefore includes stopping contributing drugs and supporting ventilation and hemodynamics, with naloxone titrated if opioid effect is clinically important.

questions.stem: Which drug class is recommended for neuropathic components after amputation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Neuropathic pain after amputation may involve peripheral nerve injury and central sensitization. Alpha-2-delta ligands such as gabapentinoids, NMDA antagonists such as ketamine, and alpha-2 agonists can target these mechanisms as components of individualized multimodal therapy.

questions.stem: A PCA patient has reached the programmed 1-hour hydromorphone limit yet continues to report severe pain. Which action BEST distinguishes undertreatment from unsafe escalation?
options: Stop the PCA and administer naloxone
Add a large basal infusion without reassessment
Reassess pain mechanism, sedation, ventilation, PCA use, and the broader analgesic plan before changing settings
questions.explanation: Reaching a PCA limit with persistent severe pain may reflect inadequate programming, a new complication, neuropathic pain, catheter or regional failure, or opioid tolerance. Reassess pain mechanism, function, sedation, ventilation, and actual PCA use before increasing settings.

questions.stem: After opioid and sedative administration, a patient becomes hypotensive with HR 50/min. Before reflexively giving another analgesic or reversal drug, which immediate assessment best characterizes the hemodynamic problem?
options: Confirm rhythm, blood pressure, perfusion, and medication context
questions.explanation: Hypotension with bradycardia has a different differential from hypotension with tachycardia. Confirming rhythm, blood pressure, perfusion, and recent medications helps distinguish drug effect, vagal physiology, conduction disease, neuraxial sympathectomy, or other causes before selecting treatment.

questions.stem: A patient with significant renal impairment requires postoperative analgesia. Which strategy BEST minimizes avoidable renal and metabolite-related risk?
options: Acetaminophen plus appropriate regional/nonopioid techniques, with individualized opioid selection if needed
Morphine PCA with a routine basal infusion
questions.explanation: Renal impairment changes both NSAID safety and the handling of opioids with renally cleared active metabolites. Acetaminophen and regional techniques can reduce systemic drug burden, while any needed opioid should be selected and titrated according to renal pharmacology and clinical response.

questions.stem: During an IV lidocaine infusion, a patient develops tinnitus and circumoral paresthesia. Which action has priority?
options: Increase the infusion because symptoms indicate inadequate effect
Stop lidocaine and evaluate immediately for local-anesthetic systemic toxicity
Continue unchanged because these are desired analgesic effects
questions.explanation: Tinnitus and circumoral paresthesia are early neurologic warning signs of local-anesthetic systemic toxicity. Stop the lidocaine infusion immediately, assess the patient, and prepare for airway, seizure, cardiovascular, and lipid-emulsion management if toxicity progresses.

questions.stem: Dexamethasone is planned for both PONV prophylaxis and a modest analgesic benefit during a several-hour case. Which timing principle best supports its use?
options: Wait until PACU because onset is immediate
Avoid it in every patient with diabetes
Administer with enough lead time for its delayed onset to contribute to the intended effects
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone has a slower onset than rapidly acting rescue antiemetics or analgesics. Giving it early enough in the case allows time for its antiemetic and modest analgesic effects to develop when they are needed postoperatively.

questions.stem: A patient with a dense peripheral nerve block is being discharged and fears severe pain when sensation returns overnight. Which instruction BEST prevents a gap in analgesia?
options: Begin the planned oral multimodal regimen before the block fully resolves
Wait until severe pain returns before taking medication
Assume the block will last at least 72 hours
Delay all medication until normal sensation is completely restored
questions.explanation: A dense single-shot block may resolve abruptly while surgical nociception persists, whereas oral medications require time to reach effect. Beginning the prescribed multimodal regimen before sensation fully returns creates overlap and reduces severe rebound pain.

questions.stem: A chronic-pain patient takes gabapentin daily and has a neuropathic component to the expected postoperative pain. Which perioperative approach best avoids an unnecessary gap in multimodal therapy?
options: Stop it routinely one week before surgery
Consider continuing/resuming gabapentin as part of the individualized plan
questions.explanation: A chronic gabapentin regimen may contribute to control of an established neuropathic pain component. Perioperative continuation or resumption should be deliberately considered with renal function, sedation, respiratory risk, and concurrent opioids rather than omitted unintentionally.

questions.stem: A highly opioid-tolerant patient is rotated to methadone after poor response to escalating doses of another opioid. Which property may make methadone useful beyond simple mu agonism?
options: It is a mixed mu antagonist-kappa agonist
NMDA-receptor antagonism may help address tolerance/hyperalgesic mechanisms
It depends primarily on renal activation
questions.explanation: Methadone combines mu-opioid agonism with NMDA-receptor antagonism, a property that may be useful when tolerance, central sensitization, or opioid-induced hyperalgesia complicates analgesia. Its variable long half-life and complex conversion still require cautious specialist-level dosing.

questions.stem: A thoracic epidural provides excellent analgesia but the patient becomes hypotensive. Which mechanism should be assessed along with intravascular volume?
questions.explanation: Thoracic epidural local anesthetic blocks sympathetic fibers as well as sensory transmission, producing vasodilation and reduced vascular tone. Hypotension therefore requires assessment of block-related sympathectomy together with intravascular volume and other hemodynamic causes.

questions.stem: A chronic-opioid patient is scheduled for major surgery. Which preoperative step is MOST important before designing supplemental intraoperative and postoperative opioid doses?
options: Determine the baseline daily opioid requirement/equivalent and build a multimodal plan around it
Stop opioids for 48 hours to reduce tolerance
Assume regional anesthesia eliminates the baseline requirement
Give naltrexone to rapidly reverse tolerance
questions.explanation: Supplemental perioperative dosing cannot be planned safely until the patient's baseline opioid exposure is known. Determine drug, formulation, daily dose, timing, and an appropriate equivalent, preserve baseline needs, then layer procedure-specific multimodal analgesia on top.

questions.stem: A continuous peripheral nerve catheter becomes disconnected, and a previously comfortable patient develops abrupt severe pain. Which interpretation BEST guides treatment?
options: The abrupt pain is the expected course and needs no intervention
Loss of continuous regional analgesia caused return or rebound of pain; restore/troubleshoot the block while providing bridge analgesia
Stopping local anesthetic caused opioid toxicity
The event indicates local-anesthetic systemic toxicity
questions.explanation: Abrupt pain after disconnection of a previously effective continuous catheter strongly suggests loss of regional drug delivery. Troubleshoot or restore the catheter when appropriate while providing bridge analgesia so the patient is not left untreated during re-establishment of the block.

questions.stem: A young woman with high PONV risk undergoes laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Which analgesic strategy BEST addresses both pain and a major modifiable PONV contributor?
options: Use high-dose systemic opioid with a basal PCA
Use opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia with appropriate antiemetic prophylaxis
Use morphine PCA as the primary strategy
questions.explanation: Opioid exposure is a modifiable contributor to postoperative nausea and vomiting. Regional and nonopioid multimodal analgesia can reduce opioid requirements, while risk-appropriate antiemetic prophylaxis addresses the patient's high baseline PONV susceptibility.

questions.stem: After bowel surgery, a patient describes diffuse cramping abdominal pain that is difficult to localize and occasionally referred away from the operative site. Which pain type best fits?
questions.explanation: Visceral pain from hollow or solid organs is often diffuse, cramping, poorly localized, and capable of referral to distant somatic regions. This pattern contrasts with the sharper, better-localized pain of superficial somatic injury.

questions.stem: A patient has shooting pain along the leg after spine surgery. What type is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Shooting pain that follows a peripheral nerve or root distribution after spine surgery suggests neuropathic pain from somatosensory nerve injury or irritation. It should be distinguished from ordinary deep somatic incisional pain because treatment mechanisms differ.

questions.stem: A long-term opioid user reports progressively worse diffuse pain as opioid doses are repeatedly increased. Which possibility should prompt a change in strategy rather than automatic dose escalation?
options: Expected improvement from higher opioid exposure
A need for mixed agonist-antagonists in every patient
questions.explanation: Worsening diffuse pain despite repeated opioid escalation raises concern for tolerance, progression of the underlying condition, or opioid-induced hyperalgesia. The appropriate response is reassessment of mechanism and multimodal strategy rather than assuming every increase in pain requires more of the same opioid.

questions.stem: A PACU patient has severe acute postoperative pain but will also need sustained analgesia after initial titration. Which prescribing principle is most appropriate?
options: Use only long-acting opioid so reassessment is unnecessary
Every PACU patient requires both a short- and long-acting opioid
Use a titratable rescue strategy for immediate pain and establish longer-lasting multimodal analgesia appropriate to the procedure and patient
Avoid nonopioid analgesia when opioids are prescribed
questions.explanation: Severe immediate PACU pain often needs a rapidly titratable rescue therapy so effect and adverse events can be assessed quickly. Sustained control should then come from longer-lasting, procedure-appropriate multimodal or regional analgesia rather than automatically relying on a long-acting opioid.

questions.stem: An epidural infusion contains both local anesthetic and opioid. Compared with a local-anesthetic-only technique, which postoperative safety issue requires particular attention?
options: Loss of all motor function regardless of concentration
No additional monitoring issue once PACU discharge criteria are met
Respiratory depression from neuraxial opioid exposure
questions.explanation: Adding an opioid to an epidural changes the adverse-effect profile because neuraxial opioid exposure can produce pruritus, nausea, urinary retention, sedation, and respiratory depression, including delayed effects with hydrophilic drugs. Monitoring must therefore reflect both local-anesthetic and opioid components.

questions.stem: A family asks why aggressive but safe postoperative pain control matters beyond comfort. Which answer BEST connects analgesia to recovery?
options: Uncontrolled pain can impair pulmonary, cardiovascular, functional, and overall recovery
Pain control changes comfort but not physiologic outcomes
Analgesia primarily shortens the operation itself
Treating pain generally delays mobilization and recovery
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled postoperative pain can impair deep breathing and cough, increase sympathetic cardiovascular stress, limit mobility and rehabilitation, disturb sleep, and delay overall recovery. Effective analgesia is therefore a functional and physiologic recovery intervention as well as a comfort measure.
